title: Maximum Subarray
description:
# Maximum Subarray

Given an integer array `nums`, return the largest possible sum of a **non-empty contiguous subarray**.

A subarray must use adjacent elements from the original array. You may not skip elements inside the chosen range, and you must choose at least one element even when every number is negative.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4]
**Output:** 6
**Explanation:** The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum 6.

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [1]
**Output:** 1
**Explanation:** The only non-empty subarray is [1].

## Example 3:

**Input:** nums = [5,4,-1,7,8]
**Output:** 23
**Explanation:** The whole array has the largest sum.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 100000`
* `-10000 <= nums[i] <= 10000`

solutions.name: Kadane's Rolling Ending Sum
solutions.description:
## Approach

Track `current`, the best sum of a non-empty subarray that must end at the current index. For each number, either extend the previous ending subarray or start a new subarray at this number. Track the largest `current` value as `best`.

## Key Insight

Any optimal subarray ending at index `i` either contains the optimal ending subarray from `i - 1` or discards it completely. If the previous ending sum hurts the total, restarting is the only useful choice.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: DP Array of Ending Sums
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store `dp[i]` as the best sum of a non-empty subarray ending exactly at index `i`. The transition is the same as Kadane's algorithm, but the full table is kept to make the dynamic programming state visible for teaching and debugging.

## Key Insight

The DP state is local: to compute the best subarray ending at `i`, only the best subarray ending at `i - 1` matters. Keeping all states shows why the rolling version is valid.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(n)

solutions.name: Prefix Sum Minus Minimum Prefix
solutions.description:
## Approach

Scan prefix sums. A subarray ending at the current position equals `prefix - earlierPrefix`, so the best ending here uses the smallest prefix sum seen before the current position. Update the answer before adding the current prefix to the minimum set for future positions.

## Key Insight

Maximum subarray can be viewed as the largest difference between two prefix sums with the smaller prefix appearing first. This explains why the chosen subarray must stay contiguous.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)

solutions.name: Divide and Conquer Crossing Sum
solutions.description:
## Approach

Recursively split the array. The best subarray is either fully in the left half, fully in the right half, or crosses the midpoint. The crossing case is the best suffix sum of the left half plus the best prefix sum of the right half.

## Key Insight

The divide-and-conquer proof separates the only three possible locations of the optimal subarray. It is slower than Kadane's algorithm but useful for understanding the interval structure.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n log n)
- Space Complexity: O(log n)

solutions.name: Segment State Monoid Merge
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent a segment by four values: total sum, best prefix sum, best suffix sum, and best subarray sum. Merge states from left to right, treating each single number as a one-element segment. The final state's best subarray sum is the answer.

## Key Insight

This is the same information a segment tree node would store. It teaches a reusable merge formula and explains how maximum subarray queries can be generalized beyond a single scan.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(n)
- Space Complexity: O(1)
